newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: ATHLETICS-CAPOBIANCO NEEDS NEW EVIDENCE, SAYS RULING BODY.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-CAPOBIANCO NEEDS NEW EVIDENCE, SAYS RULING BODY.

text.p: Australian sprinter Dean Capobianco will damage athletics if he fights a four-year ban for a positive drug test without new evidence, his national ruling body said on Tuesday.
Capobianco has said he would apply to the International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) to have the ban overturned after repeatedly stating his innocence.

But Athletics Australia (AA) said the case has been properly heard and, as it stands, it would not be in the sport's interests for Capobianco to further challenge the IAAF ruling, which was announced in Monte Carlo on Monday.
"I think a continuation of the case clearly would not be good for the sport," AA president Terry Dwyer told Reuters.
"Unless new evidence is presented, it would just be bad publicity. From what we can see, the case itself is one that has been well heard," he said.
"But Dean has the right as an individual to pursue it if he believes he needs to do that."

In announcing the ban, the IAAF said Capobianco tested positive for the anabolic steroid stanozolol at a meeting in the Netherlands last May. The 26-year-old sprinter escaped an automatic four-year ban when a subsequent AA tribunal cleared him on the grounds that the testing procedures had been seriously flawed. The IAAF opposed that decision.
Speaking to reporters in London after flying from Monte Carlo, Capobianco said he did not believe it was his sample which contained the banned substances and described the ruling as "disgraceful".
Dwyer said the IAAF hearing, which overruled AA's earlier ruling, was fair but called for improvements in drug testing procedures.
"I think they can be tightened up. But that's not to say in this case a lack of tightness resulted in a wrong decision," Dwyer said.
"..we cannot support him (Capobianco) in the sense of saying he's innocent or that he's not guilty. That's not our role. Our role is to see it's done fairly," he said.
The IAAF ban will keep Capobianco out of official competition until only a few months before the 2000 Olympics in Sydney.
